claim: Nine healthy volunteers (5 female, age 25 ± 3 years) participated in the study.
source: Nine healthy volunteers (5F, age 25 ± 3 yrs) participated in the study.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript describing the study participants.

claim: All participants were right-handed according to the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory.
source: The subjects were right-handed according to the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (Oldfield, 1971).
evidence: Direct statement with citation to the handedness assessment method.

claim: The kinematic synergy model achieved an average discrimination accuracy of 91.1 ± 3.6% for hand postures.
source: All the three models were able to significantly distinguish between individual hand postures (average accuracy ± standard deviation -SD-; chance level: 50%; kinematic synergy: 91.1 ± 3.6%; individual digit: 85.9 ± 5%; muscle synergy: 72 ± 7.7%) (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Quantitative results from behavioral validation procedure.

claim: The individual digit model achieved an average discrimination accuracy of 85.9 ± 5% for hand postures.
source: All the three models were able to significantly distinguish between individual hand postures (average accuracy ± standard deviation -SD-; chance level: 50%; kinematic synergy: 91.1 ± 3.6%; individual digit: 85.9 ± 5%; muscle synergy: 72 ± 7.7%) (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Quantitative results from behavioral validation procedure.

claim: The muscle synergy model achieved an average discrimination accuracy of 72 ± 7.7% for hand postures.
source: All the three models were able to significantly distinguish between individual hand postures (average accuracy ± standard deviation -SD-; chance level: 50%; kinematic synergy: 91.1 ± 3.6%; individual digit: 85.9 ± 5%; muscle synergy: 72 ± 7.7%) (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Quantitative results from behavioral validation procedure.

claim: The kinematic synergy model performed significantly better than both the individual digit and muscle synergy models in discriminating hand postures.
source: Specifically, the kinematic synergy model performed significantly better than both the individual digit and muscle synergy models while the individual digit model was significantly more informative than the muscle synergy model (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p<0.05, Bonferroni-Holm corrected).
evidence: Statistical comparison with specified test and correction method.

claim: The individual digit model was significantly more informative than the muscle synergy model in discriminating hand postures.
source: Specifically, the kinematic synergy model performed significantly better than both the individual digit and muscle synergy models while the individual digit model was significantly more informative than the muscle synergy model (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p<0.05, Bonferroni-Holm corrected).
evidence: Statistical comparison with specified test and correction method.

claim: The encoding procedure based on the kinematic synergy model was successful across all participants with an average accuracy of 71.58 ± 5.52%.
source: Overall, the encoding procedure based on the kinematic synergy model was highly successful across all participants (average accuracy ± SD: 71.58 ± 5.52%) and always significantly above chance level (see Supplementary file 1B for single subject results).
evidence: Quantitative results from fMRI encoding analysis.

claim: The encoding of the individual digit model was successful in five of nine participants only with an average accuracy of 63.89 ± 6.86%.
source: The encoding of the individual digit model was successful in five of nine participants only (63.89 ± 6.86%).
evidence: Quantitative results from fMRI encoding analysis.

claim: The muscle synergy model successfully predicted brain activity in six out of eight participants with an average accuracy of 63.9 ± 6.5%.
source: Finally, the muscle synergy model successfully predicted brain activity in six out of eight participants, with an average accuracy that was comparable to the individual digit model (63.9 ± 6.5%).
evidence: Quantitative results from fMRI encoding analysis.

claim: The kinematic synergy model outperformed both the individual digit and the muscle synergy models in predicting brain activity.
source: The kinematic synergy model outperformed both the individual digit and the muscle synergy models (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p<0.05, Bonferroni-Holm corrected), whereas no significant difference was found between the individual digit and muscle synergy models (p=0.95).
evidence: Statistical comparison with specified test and correction method.

claim: No significant difference was found between the individual digit and muscle synergy models in predicting brain activity.
source: The kinematic synergy model outperformed both the individual digit and the muscle synergy models (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p<0.05, Bonferroni-Holm corrected), whereas no significant difference was found between the individual digit and muscle synergy models (p=0.95).
evidence: Statistical comparison with specified p-value.

claim: 40.8% of the BOLD signal was accounted for by the kinematic synergies.
source: Therefore, 40.8% of the BOLD signal was accounted for by the kinematic synergies, whereas the two other behavioral models explained a relatively smaller fraction of the total variance.
evidence: Quantitative measure of model fit to fMRI data.

claim: The group average R² coefficient between fMRI data and kinematic synergies was 0.41 ± 0.06.
source: The group averages were 0.41 ± 0.06 for the kinematic synergies, 0.37 ± 0.03 for the individual digits, and 0.37 ± 0.06 for the muscle synergies.
evidence: Quantitative measure of model fit to fMRI data.

claim: The group average R² coefficient between fMRI data and individual digits was 0.37 ± 0.03.
source: The group averages were 0.41 ± 0.06 for the kinematic synergies, 0.37 ± 0.03 for the individual digits, and 0.37 ± 0.06 for the muscle synergies.
evidence: Quantitative measure of model fit to fMRI data.

claim: The group average R² coefficient between fMRI data and muscle synergies was 0.37 ± 0.06.
source: The group averages were 0.41 ± 0.06 for the kinematic synergies, 0.37 ± 0.03 for the individual digits, and 0.37 ± 0.06 for the muscle synergies.
evidence: Quantitative measure of model fit to fMRI data.

claim: The hand-posture-related network comprises bilateral precentral cortex, supplementary motor area (SMA), ventral premotor and supramarginal areas, and left inferior parietal and postcentral cortex.
source: The group-level probability map, which displays the voxels recruited in at least four subjects, consisted of a well-recognizable network of hand-related regions, specifically bilateral precentral cortex, supplementary motor area (SMA), ventral premotor and supramarginal areas, left inferior parietal and postcentral cortex (Figure 1; coordinates in Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: Group-level fMRI analysis results with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The first three kinematic principal components can explain more than 80% of the variance across the entire hand kinematic dataset.
source: For visualization purposes, we focused on the first three PCs, which could explain more than 80% of the variance across the entire hand kinematic dataset, and were also highly consistent across participants (Video 1).
evidence: Quantitative measure of variance explained by principal components.

claim: The first synergy modulates abduction-adduction and flexion-extension of both the proximal and distal finger joints.
source: It can be observed that the first synergy modulates abduction-adduction and flexion-extension of both the proximal and distal finger joints, while the second synergy reflects thumb opposition and flexion-extension of the distal joints only.
evidence: Description of kinematic synergy characteristics from Video 1.

claim: The second synergy reflects thumb opposition and flexion-extension of the distal joints only.
source: It can be observed that the first synergy modulates abduction-adduction and flexion-extension of both the proximal and distal finger joints, while the second synergy reflects thumb opposition and flexion-extension of the distal joints only.
evidence: Description of kinematic synergy characteristics from Video 1.

claim: Maximizing the first synergy leads to a posture resembling a power grasp.
source: Maximizing the first synergy leads, therefore, to a posture resembling a power grasp, while the second one is linked to pinch movements directed towards smaller objects, and the third one represents movements of flexion and thumb opposition (like in grasping a dish or a platter) (Santello et al., 1998; Gentner and Classen, 2006; Ingram et al., 2008; Thakur et al., 2008).
evidence: Description of synergy function with supporting citations.

claim: The second synergy is linked to pinch movements directed towards smaller objects.
source: Maximizing the first synergy leads, therefore, to a posture resembling a power grasp, while the second one is linked to pinch movements directed towards smaller objects, and the third one represents movements of flexion and thumb opposition (like in grasping a dish or a platter) (Santello et al., 1998; Gentner and Classen, 2006; Ingram et al., 2008; Thakur et al., 2008).
evidence: Description of synergy function with supporting citations.

claim: The third synergy represents movements of flexion and thumb opposition like in grasping a dish or a platter.
source: Maximizing the first synergy leads, therefore, to a posture resembling a power grasp, while the second one is linked to pinch movements directed towards smaller objects, and the third one represents movements of flexion and thumb opposition (like in grasping a dish or a platter) (Santello et al., 1998; Gentner and Classen, 2006; Ingram et al., 2008; Thakur et al., 2008).
evidence: Description of synergy function with supporting citations.

claim: The group kinematic synergies are represented in the precentral and postcentral cortex in distinct clusters arranged in a topographical continuum with smooth supero-inferior transitions.
source: Figure 2 shows that the group kinematic synergies are represented in the precentral and postcentral cortex in distinct clusters that are arranged in a topographical continuum with smooth supero-inferior transitions.
evidence: Description of cortical mapping results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The topographical arrangement of synergies was statistically significant (C=0.19; p=0.038).
source: The procedure developed to assess the topographical arrangement of synergies (see Materials and methods) was statistically significant (C=0.19; p=0.038), indicating that anatomically close voxels exhibited similar synergy coefficients (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical test result for topographical organization.

claim: Anatomically close voxels exhibited similar synergy coefficients.
source: The procedure developed to assess the topographical arrangement of synergies (see Materials and methods) was statistically significant (C=0.19; p=0.038), indicating that anatomically close voxels exhibited similar synergy coefficients (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Interpretation of statistical test result.

claim: All group correlations between fMRI and behavioral data and between behavioral models were highly significant (p<0.0001).
source: All group correlations, both between fMRI and behavioral data and between behavioral models were highly significant (p<0.0001) (for details see Supplementary file 1D,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical results from representational similarity analysis.

claim: The goodness-of-fit (R²) between the original and reconstructed joint angle patterns related to single movements, averaged across subjects, ranged between 0.51 and 0.90.
source: The goodness-of-fit (R2) between the original and reconstructed joint angle patterns related to single movements, averaged across subjects, ranged between 0.51 and 0.90 (Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: Quantitative results from decoding analysis.

claim: The rank accuracy procedure for decoded postures yielded significant results in six of nine participants.
source: Moreover, the rank accuracy procedure specifically designed to test the extent to which each decoded posture could be discriminated from the original ones yielded significant results in six of nine participants (Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: Statistical results from decoding validation procedure.

claim: The encoding procedure using the kinematic synergy model with visual object presentation activity was unsuccessful in all participants.
source: The procedure was unsuccessful in all participants, thus indicating that the kinematic synergy information in motor and premotor regions was purely related to motor activity (Supplementary file 1H).
evidence: Control analysis results excluding visual contribution.

claim: The kinematic synergy information in motor and premotor regions was purely related to motor activity.
source: The procedure was unsuccessful in all participants, thus indicating that the kinematic synergy information in motor and premotor regions was purely related to motor activity (Supplementary file 1H).
evidence: Interpretation of control analysis results.

claim: Visual areas encoding analysis results were at chance level in seven out of nine participants.
source: The results were at the chance level in seven out of nine participants (see Supplementary file 1I), suggesting that visual imagery processes in the occipital cortex did not retain kinematic synergy information.
evidence: Control analysis results for visual areas.

claim: Visual imagery processes in the occipital cortex did not retain kinematic synergy information.
source: The results were at the chance level in seven out of nine participants (see Supplementary file 1I), suggesting that visual imagery processes in the occipital cortex did not retain kinematic synergy information.
evidence: Interpretation of control analysis results.

claim: The human hand is capable of performing a strikingly wide range of movements characterized by a high degree of adaptability and dexterity.
source: Unique among primates, the human hand is capable of performing a strikingly wide range of movements, characterized by a high degree of adaptability and dexterity that enables complex interactions with the environment.
evidence: General statement about human hand capabilities.

claim: The multiple ways in which the hand can perform a given goal-directed movement arise from anatomical, functional, and kinematic redundancies.
source: The multiple ways in which the hand can perform a given goal-directed movement arise from anatomical, functional, and kinematic redundancies, i.e., a large number of degrees of freedom (DoFs) (Bernstein, 1967).
evidence: Statement about hand redundancy with citation.

claim: Synergies represent functional sensorimotor modules that result from the combination of elementary variables and behave as single functional units.
source: From a theoretical perspective, synergies represent functional sensorimotor modules that result from the combination of elementary variables and behave as single functional units (Turvey, 2007; Latash, 2010).
evidence: Definition of synergies with supporting citations.

claim: Kinematic synergies correspond to covariation patterns in finger joint angles and are quantified through kinematic recordings.
source: Kinematic synergies correspond to covariation patterns in finger joint angles and are quantified through kinematic recordings (Santello et al., 1998; Gabiccini et al., 2013; Tessitore et al., 2013).
evidence: Definition of kinematic synergies with supporting citations.

claim: Muscle synergies represent covariation patterns in finger muscle activations and are typically extracted from electromyography (EMG) signals.
source: Muscle synergies represent covariation patterns in finger muscle activations and are typically extracted from electromyography (EMG) signals (Weiss and Flanders, 2004; d'Avella and Lacquaniti, 2013).
evidence: Definition of muscle synergies with supporting citations.

claim: Three hand postural synergies identified through principal component analysis accounted for more than 84% of variance in kinematic data across all hand postures.
source: Three hand postural synergies were identified through a principal component analysis (PCA) that accounted for a high fraction (>84%) of variance in the kinematic data across all hand postures and characterized hand configurations as linear combinations of finger joints (Santello et al., 1998).
evidence: Citation to previous study results.

claim: Synergistic/dexterous and non-synergistic hand movements elicited different neural responses in the premotor and parietal network that controls hand posture.
source: For instance, in a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) study, synergistic/dexterous and non-synergistic hand movements elicited different neural responses in the premotor and parietal network that controls hand posture (Ehrsson et al., 2002).
evidence: Citation to previous fMRI study.

claim: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) induced hand movements encompassed within distinct postural synergies.
source: Equally, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) induced hand movements encompassed within distinct postural synergies (Gentner and Classen, 2006).
evidence: Citation to previous TMS study.

claim: Classic somatotopic theories postulated that distinct clusters of neuronal populations are associated with specific hand muscles, fingers, or finger movements.
source: Above all, classic somatotopic theories postulated that distinct clusters of neuronal populations are associated with specific hand muscles, fingers, or finger movements (Penfield and Boldrey, 1937; Penfield and Rasmussen, 1950; Woolsey et al., 1952).
evidence: Description of classic theories with citations.

claim: In hand motor area, neurons controlling single fingers are organized in distributed, overlapping cortical patches without any detectable segregation.
source: In hand motor area, neurons controlling single fingers are organized in distributed, overlapping cortical patches without any detectable segregation (Penfield and Boldrey, 1937; Schieber, 1991, Schieber, 2001).
evidence: Statement about motor cortex organization with citations.

claim: fMRI neural activation patterns for individual digits in sensorimotor cortex are not somatotopically organized and their spatial arrangement is highly variable.
source: In addition, it has been recently shown that fMRI neural activation patterns for individual digits in sensorimotor cortex are not somatotopically organized and their spatial arrangement is highly variable, while their representational structure (i.e., the pattern of distances between digit-specific activations) is invariant across individuals (Ejaz et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to recent study findings.

claim: The representational structure of digit-specific activations is invariant across individuals.
source: In addition, it has been recently shown that fMRI neural activation patterns for individual digits in sensorimotor cortex are not somatotopically organized and their spatial arrangement is highly variable, while their representational structure (i.e., the pattern of distances between digit-specific activations) is invariant across individuals (Ejaz et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to recent study findings.

claim: Hand postural information encoded through kinematic synergies is represented in cortical areas devoted to hand motor control.
source: Hand postural information, encoded through kinematic synergies, were represented in cortical areas devoted to hand motor control and successfully discriminated individual grasping movements, significantly outperforming alternative somatotopic or muscle-based models.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Kinematic synergies successfully discriminated individual grasping movements, significantly outperforming alternative somatotopic or muscle-based models.
source: Hand postural information, encoded through kinematic synergies, were represented in cortical areas devoted to hand motor control and successfully discriminated individual grasping movements, significantly outperforming alternative somatotopic or muscle-based models.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Hand postural synergies were predicted by neural activation patterns within primary motor cortex.
source: Importantly, hand postural synergies were predicted by neural activation patterns within primary motor cortex.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The findings support a novel cortical organization for hand movement control.
source: These findings support a novel cortical organization for hand movement control and open potential applications for brain-computer interfaces and neuroprostheses.
evidence: Interpretation of findings stated in the abstract.

claim: The findings open potential applications for brain-computer interfaces and neuroprostheses.
source: These findings support a novel cortical organization for hand movement control and open potential applications for brain-computer interfaces and neuroprostheses.
evidence: Implication of findings stated in the abstract.

claim: The width of the probability maps measured on the cortical mesh was approximately 1 cm.
source: Finally, the width of our probability maps, measured on the cortical mesh, was ca. 1cm, which corresponds to the hand area, as defined by techniques with better spatial resolution, including ultra-high field fMRI or electrocorticography (ECoG) (Siero et al., 2014).
evidence: Quantitative measurement of cortical map extent.

claim: The width of the probability maps corresponds to the hand area as defined by techniques with better spatial resolution.
source: Finally, the width of our probability maps, measured on the cortical mesh, was ca. 1cm, which corresponds to the hand area, as defined by techniques with better spatial resolution, including ultra-high field fMRI or electrocorticography (ECoG) (Siero et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison with other techniques with citation.

claim: Motor and premotor regions contain neuronal populations that respond to visual stimuli.
source: Since motor and premotor regions supposedly contains neuronal populations that respond to visual stimuli (Kwan et al., 1985; Castiello, 2005; Klaes et al., 2015), one may argue that the visual presentation of objects in the current experiment contributes to the synergy-based encoding of BOLD activity in those regions.
evidence: Statement about motor cortex properties with citations.

claim: Inferior parietal and postcentral areas are engaged in higher-level processing during object interaction.
source: Inferior parietal and postcentral areas are engaged in higher-level processing during object interaction (Culham et al., 2003).
evidence: Statement about parietal cortex function with citation.

claim: Grasping movements require integration of motor information with inputs related to the target object.
source: Since grasping, as opposed to reaching movements, requires integration of motor information with inputs related to the target object, these regions may integrate the sensorimotor features needed to preshape the hand correctly (Grefkes et al., 2002; Culham et al., 2003).
evidence: Statement about grasping requirements with citations.

claim: Different tool-directed movements were decoded from brain activity in the intraparietal sulcus.
source: Consistently, different tool-directed movements were decoded from brain activity in the intraparietal sulcus (Gallivan et al., 2013), and it has been reported that this region is sensitive to differences between precision and power grasps (Ehrsson et al., 2000; Gallivan et al., 2011).
evidence: Citation to previous decoding study.

claim: The intraparietal sulcus is sensitive to differences between precision and power grasps.
source: Consistently, different tool-directed movements were decoded from brain activity in the intraparietal sulcus (Gallivan et al., 2013), and it has been reported that this region is sensitive to differences between precision and power grasps (Ehrsson et al., 2000; Gallivan et al., 2011).
evidence: Citation to previous studies.

claim: Bilateral activations of SMA were often described during motor tasks.
source: Specifically, bilateral activations of SMA were often described during motor tasks (Ehrsson et al., 2001; Ehrsson et al., 2002) and a recent meta-analysis indicated a consistent recruitment of SMA in grasp type comparisons (King et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to previous studies and meta-analysis.

claim: A bilateral, but left dominant, involvement of intraparietal cortex for grasping has been reported.
source: Equally, a bilateral, but left dominant, involvement of intraparietal cortex for grasping has been reported (Culham et al., 2003).
evidence: Citation to previous study.

claim: Action recognition and mirror mechanisms may rely on the extraction of reduced representations of gestures rather than on the observation of individual motor acts.
source: Moreover, some authors have hypothesized recently that action recognition and mirror mechanisms may rely on the extraction of reduced representations of gestures, rather than on the observation of individual motor acts (D'Ausilio et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to recent hypothesis.

claim: At least some subdomains of primary somatosensory cortex (areas 2 and 3a) contain neurons that respond to multiple digits.
source: Indeed, at least some subdomains (areas 2 and 3a) contain neurons that respond to multiple digits (Iwamura et al., 1980), despite the evidence supporting specific single finger representations in S1 (Kaas, 1983).
evidence: Citation to previous neurophysiological studies.

claim: Three and five principal components can account for at least 80% and 90% of the variance in hand kinematic data, respectively.
source: This number was selected based on previous behavioral studies that showed that three and five PCs can account for at least 80% and 90% of the variance, respectively (Santello et al., 1998, Santello et al., 2002; Weiss and Flanders, 2004; Gentner and Classen, 2006; Gentner et al., 2010; Overduin et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation to multiple previous studies.

claim: Mouse motor cortex is organized in clusters that encode different motor acts.
source: In fact, mouse motor cortex is organized in clusters that encode different motor acts (Brown and Teskey, 2014).
evidence: Citation to study in animal model.

claim: Stimulation of motor cortex in monkeys produces movements directed to stable spatial end-points.
source: Similarly, stimulation of motor cortex in monkeys produces movements directed to stable spatial end-points (Graziano et al., 2002; Aflalo and Graziano, 2006) and may have a synergistic organization (Overduin et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation to studies in animal model.

claim: Complex movements can be recorded from parietal as well as premotor and motor areas in both monkeys and humans.
source: Recently, it has been demonstrated in both monkeys and humans that complex movements can be recorded from parietal as well as premotor and motor areas (Aflalo et al., 2015; Klaes et al., 2015; Schaffelhofer et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to recent studies.

claim: Successful decoding can be achieved in parietal, premotor and motor areas both during motor planning and execution.
source: Interestingly, a successful decoding can be achieved in those regions both during motor planning and execution (Schaffelhofer et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to recent study.

claim: Individual representations of digits within M1 show a high degree of overlap.
source: These observations about the internal organization of motor cortex were demonstrated also in humans, revealing that individual representations of digits within M1 show a high degree of overlap (Indovina and Sanes, 2001) and that, despite digits may be arranged in a coarse ventro-dorsal order in somatosensory cortex, their representations are intermingled so that the existence of digit specific voxels is unlikely (Ejaz et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to previous human studies.

claim: Despite digits may be arranged in a coarse ventro-dorsal order in somatosensory cortex, their representations are intermingled so that the existence of digit specific voxels is unlikely.
source: These observations about the internal organization of motor cortex were demonstrated also in humans, revealing that individual representations of digits within M1 show a high degree of overlap (Indovina and Sanes, 2001) and that, despite digits may be arranged in a coarse ventro-dorsal order in somatosensory cortex, their representations are intermingled so that the existence of digit specific voxels is unlikely (Ejaz et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to previous human study.

claim: Individual cortical voxels may contain enough information to encode specific gestures.
source: In contrast, individual cortical voxels may contain enough information to encode specific gestures (Bleichner et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to previous study.

claim: Neural spikes in primary motor cortex can be used to control robotic limbs used for performing simple or complex movements.
source: This result yields potential applications for the development of novel brain computer interfaces: for instance, previous studies demonstrated that neural spikes in primary motor cortex can be used to control robotic limbs used for performing simple or complex movements (Schwartz et al., 2006; Schwartz, 2007; Velliste et al., 2008).
evidence: Citation to previous brain-computer interface studies.

claim: Neural activity patterns associated with grasp trajectories can be predicted from single neuron activity in M1 in monkeys.
source: Previous studies in monkeys suggest that neural activity patterns associated with grasp trajectories can be predicted from single neuron activity in M1 (Saleh et al., 2010; Saleh et al., 2012; Schaffelhofer et al., 2015) and recently neuronal spikes have been associated with principal components (Mollazadeh et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to studies in animal models.

claim: Neuronal spikes have been associated with principal components.
source: Previous studies in monkeys suggest that neural activity patterns associated with grasp trajectories can be predicted from single neuron activity in M1 (Saleh et al., 2010; Saleh et al., 2012; Schaffelhofer et al., 2015) and recently neuronal spikes have been associated with principal components (Mollazadeh et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to recent study.

claim: Cortical activity obtained through intracranial recordings can be used to decode postural information in humans.
source: In humans, cortical activity obtained through intracranial recordings can be used to decode postural information (Pistohl et al., 2012) and proper techniques can even lead to decode EMG activity from fMRI patterns (Ganesh et al., 2008) or from ECoG signals (Flint et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to previous human studies.

claim: EMG activity can be decoded from fMRI patterns.
source: In humans, cortical activity obtained through intracranial recordings can be used to decode postural information (Pistohl et al., 2012) and proper techniques can even lead to decode EMG activity from fMRI patterns (Ganesh et al., 2008) or from ECoG signals (Flint et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to previous study.

claim: EMG activity can be decoded from ECoG signals.
source: In humans, cortical activity obtained through intracranial recordings can be used to decode postural information (Pistohl et al., 2012) and proper techniques can even lead to decode EMG activity from fMRI patterns (Ganesh et al., 2008) or from ECoG signals (Flint et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to previous study.

claim: Decoding of actual posture from fMRI activity in M1 was possible at individual voxel level with simplified paradigms and supervised classifiers that identified only four different movements.
source: So far, decoding of actual posture from fMRI activity in M1 was possible at individual voxel level, albeit with simplified paradigms and supervised classifiers that identified only four different movements (Bleichner et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to previous study.

claim: A set of few synergies can describe hand posture in a reliable way, obtaining hand postures that correlated highly with those recorded with optical tracking.
source: Other authors similarly demonstrated that a set of few synergies can describe hand posture in a reliable way, obtaining hand postures that correlated highly with those recorded with optical tracking (Thakur et al., 2008).
evidence: Citation to previous study.

claim: The study sample size is comparable to that of most reports on motor control and posture.
source: While nine subjects may appear to be a relatively limited sample for a fMRI study, our study sample is comparable to that of most reports on motor control and posture (e.g., Santello et al., 1998; Weiss and Flanders, 2004; Ingram et al., 2008; Thakur et al., 2008; Tessitore et al., 2013; Ejaz et al., 2015) as well as to the sample size of fMRI studies that use encoding techniques, rather than univariate analyses (Mitchell et al., 2008; Huth et al., 2012).
evidence: Comparison with previous studies with citations.

claim: When motor acts were performed toward both real and imagined objects, the results obtained from synergy evaluation were highly similar.
source: Moreover, when motor acts were performed toward both real and imagined objects, the results obtained from synergy evaluation were highly similar (Santello et al., 2002).
evidence: Citation to previous study comparing real and imagined objects.

claim: The first few principal components could explain most of the variance across a very wide number of motor acts despite wide variety of experimental settings.
source: Interestingly, the dimensionality reduction methods were adopted with high consistency in these reports, despite the wide variety of experimental settings, and the first few PCs could explain most of the variance across a very wide number of motor acts.
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple previous studies.

claim: EMG recordings with higher dimensionality or different signal processing do not lead to better discrimination results.
source: The results, reported in the Appendix, demonstrate that EMG recordings with a higher dimensionality (Gazzoni et al., 2014; Muceli et al., 2014) or a different signal processing (Ejaz et al., 2015) do not lead to better discrimination results.
evidence: Results from additional analysis with citations.

claim: The worst performance of the muscle model relates more to the signal-to-noise ratio of the EMG technique per se, rather than to shortcomings of either the acquisition device or the signal processing methods.
source: These findings are consistent with previous reports (Muceli et al., 2014), and indicate that, in the current study, the worst performance of the muscle model relates more to the signal-to-noise ratio of the EMG technique per se, rather than to shortcomings of either the acquisition device or the signal processing methods adopted here.
evidence: Interpretation of additional analysis results with citation.

claim: Only a portion (40%) of the total brain activity could be accounted for by kinematic synergies.
source: In our data, only a portion (40%) of the total brain activity could be accounted for by kinematic synergies.
evidence: Quantitative measure of model fit limitation.

claim: Only a small fraction of variance in M1 is related to arm posture.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that only a small fraction of variance in M1 is related to arm posture (Aflalo and Graziano, 2006) and that grasping force can be efficiently decoded from electrical activity, suggesting that at least a subset of M1 neurons processes force-related information (Flint et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to previous studies.

claim: Grasping force can be efficiently decoded from electrical activity, suggesting that at least a subset of M1 neurons processes force-related information.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that only a small fraction of variance in M1 is related to arm posture (Aflalo and Graziano, 2006) and that grasping force can be efficiently decoded from electrical activity, suggesting that at least a subset of M1 neurons processes force-related information (Flint et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to previous study with interpretation.

claim: Motor areas can combine individual digit patterns on the basis of alternative non-synergistic or nonlinear combinations.
source: In addition, motor areas can combine individual digit patterns on the basis of alternative non-synergistic or nonlinear combinations and the correlated activity patterns for adjacent fingers may depend on alternative mechanisms such as finger enslaving (Ejaz et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to previous study.

claim: Correlated activity patterns for adjacent fingers may depend on alternative mechanisms such as finger enslaving.
source: In addition, motor areas can combine individual digit patterns on the basis of alternative non-synergistic or nonlinear combinations and the correlated activity patterns for adjacent fingers may depend on alternative mechanisms such as finger enslaving (Ejaz et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to previous study.

claim: Studies in animal models bear strong evidence for a distributed coding of hand synergies beyond motor cortex, i.e., spinal cord.
source: It should also be noted that studies in animal models bear strong evidence for a distributed coding of hand synergies beyond motor cortex, i.e., spinal cord (Overduin et al., 2012; Santello et al., 2013).
evidence: Citation to studies in animal models.

claim: According to the redundancy principle, only a part of M1 neurons may be directly implied in movement or posture control.
source: According to the redundancy principle, only a part of M1 neurons may be directly implied in movement or posture control (Latash et al., 2007), whereas the remaining neurons may deal with force production or posture adjustments and control over time, allowing for the high flexibility and adaptability which are peculiar features of human hand movements.
evidence: Statement about motor control principle with citation.

claim: The kinematic data were acquired from the motion capture experiment using an optical motion capture system composed of ten stereocameras with a sampling frequency of 480 Hz.
source: Hand posture was measured by an optical motion capture system (Phase Space, San Leandro, CA, USA), composed of ten stereocameras with a sampling frequency of 480 Hz.
evidence: Description of data acquisition method.

claim: The kinematic model consists of 26 Degrees of Freedom (DoFs), 24 pertaining to the hand and 2 to the wrist.
source: The placement of the markers was performed according to the model described in Gabiccini et al., 2013, which consists of 26 Degrees of Freedom (DoFs), 24 pertaining to the hand and 2 to the wrist.
evidence: Description of kinematic model with citation.

claim: EMG signals were recorded from five different muscles: flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS), extensor digitorum communis (EDC), first dorsal interosseus (FDI), abductor pollicis brevis (APB), and abductor digiti minimi (ADM).
source: EMG signals were acquired from five different muscles using self-adhesive surface electrodes. The muscles used for recording were: flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS), extensor digitorum communis (EDC), first dorsal interosseus (FDI), abductor pollicis brevis (APB), and abductor digiti minimi (ADM).
evidence: Description of EMG data acquisition.

claim: EMG signals were sampled at 2 kHz.
source: EMG signals were sampled at 2 kHz.
evidence: Technical specification of data acquisition.

claim: Functional data were acquired with a 3.0 Tesla GE Signa scanner equipped with an 8-channel head-only coil.
source: Functional data were acquired with a 3.0 Tesla GE Signa scanner (GE, Milwaukee, WI, USA), equipped with an 8-channel head-only coil.
evidence: Description of fMRI acquisition equipment.

claim: A Gradient-Echo echo-planar sequence was used with TR = 2.5 s, TE = 40 ms, and FA = 90°.
source: A Gradient-Echo echo-planar sequence was used, with an acquisition matrix of 128 x 128, FOV = 240 x 240 mm, Repetition Time (TR) = 2.5 s, Time of Echo (TE) = 40 ms, Flip Angle (FA) = 90°.
evidence: Technical specifications of fMRI acquisition.

claim: Each fMRI volume comprised 43 3 mm-thick slices and the resulting voxel size was 1.875 x 1.875 x 3 mm.
source: Each volume comprised 43 3 mm-thick slices and the resulting voxel size was 1.875 x 1.875 x 3 mm.
evidence: Technical specifications of fMRI acquisition.

claim: Twenty different objects were used in the current study.
source: Twenty different objects, chosen from our previous report (Santello et al., 1998), were used in the current study (see Supplementary file 1J for a list).
evidence: Description of experimental stimuli with citation.

claim: The experiment was organized in five runs, each composed by twenty trials, in randomized order across participants.
source: The experiment was organized in five runs, each composed by twenty trials, in randomized order across participants.
evidence: Description of experimental design.

claim: All the grasp-to-use movements were performed five times.
source: Therefore, all the grasp-to-use movements were performed five times.
evidence: Description of experimental design.

claim: The encoding procedure consisted in 190 iterations of a leave-two-out cross-validation.
source: The procedure consisted in 190 iterations of a leave-two-out cross-validation in which the stimuli were first partitioned in a training set (18 stimuli) and a test set with the two left-out examples.
evidence: Description of analysis method.

claim: The sample for the encoding analysis was restricted to the 5000 voxels with the best average BOLD response across the 18 stimuli in the training set.
source: The sample for the analysis was then restricted to the 5000 voxels with the best average BOLD response across the 18 stimuli in the training set (expressed by the highest t-scores).
evidence: Description of analysis method.

claim: After training the model, only the 1000 voxels that showed the highest R² were retained.
source: After training the model, only the 1000 voxels that showed the highest R2 (a measure of fitting between the matrix of synergy weights and the training data) were retained.
evidence: Description of analysis method.

claim: A cluster size correction (nearest neighbor, size = 50 voxels) was applied to prune small, isolated clusters of voxels.
source: A cluster size correction (nearest neighbor, size = 50 voxels) was also applied to prune small, isolated clusters of voxels.
evidence: Description of analysis method.

claim: A probability threshold of p>0.33 was applied on the maps to retain voxels in which the encoding procedure was successful in at least four out of the nine subjects.
source: Moreover, a probability threshold of these maps (p>0.33) was applied on the maps to retain voxels in which the encoding procedure was successful in at least four out of the nine subjects (Figure 1).
evidence: Description of group analysis method.
